open_obligations: Check that a stochastic oracle with constant advantage over random guessing is an adequate model of human error.
Note the authors themselves leave oracles with systematic errors on some queries open.
Check whether the efficient-honest-prover requirement changes the class of decidable problems relative to PSPACE.
out.other_title: Debate is a proposal only for natural language; theory assumes error-free judges
out.rationale: Irving et al. note their theory models judges as error-free and agents as unbounded and call for richer models. Brown-Cohen et al. require the honest prover to run in polynomial time and, in Theorem 6.2, allow a stochastic human-judgement oracle (K-Lipschitz machine, O(K^2) queries, completeness 3/5, soundness 2/5), which relaxes both assumptions partially; the dishonest prover is still unbounded and the oracle is not allowed arbitrary errors.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate theory can drop the error-free judge and unbounded debaters of the DEBATE = PSPACE analogy, for oracle machines with a stochastic human-judgement oracle

open_obligations: Check whether the K-Lipschitz assumption excludes the chaotic simulations Irving et al. worry about.
Confirm that the protocol handles adversarially chosen noise at each step, the failure mode Irving et al. describe.
Check whether cross-examination is practical for the debaters in question.
out.other_title: Open: debate protocol for stochastic simulation (bisection works only if deterministic)
out.rationale: Irving et al. leave open a natural debate protocol for stochastic simulation, since bisection only works for deterministic simulation. Theorem 6.2 of Brown-Cohen et al. gives a protocol for K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machines in which A proposes the probability of each next bit and the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, with O(K^2) oracle queries, completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5; the guarantee needs the Lipschitz condition and cross-examination.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate can efficiently verify stochastic computations, for probabilistic oracle machines that are K-Lipschitz at the human-judgement oracle

text: Theorem 6.2 states that any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machine in time T with query length l has an (O(K^2 T log T), O(K^2 + l log T), O(K^2))-debate protocol with cross-examination deciding it with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5. A proposes the probability of each next bit, the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, and if B aborts the verifier samples the human oracle to check A's probability; the authors say savings are non-trivial when K = o(sqrt T), most interestingly K = O(1).
title: Theorem 6.2: stochastic-oracle doubly-efficient debate with O(K^2) human queries
